# Buyer Offer Panel

Compare what potential buyers understand, value, question, and would consider doing about an offer. Recommend what to advance, improve, or validate with real customers.

This file is self-contained. Use the host's research, agent, computation, and artifact tools. Qualitative comparison needs no embedding service. Optional semantic similarity rating (SSR) requires actual embeddings and computation. Synthetic reactions generate hypotheses; they do not establish demand or predict conversion.

## 1. Define the decision and outcome

Extract the target, variants, intended audience, constraints, and decision from the request. Infer sensible defaults and label assumptions. Ask one focused question only when missing information prevents useful work. Continue useful comparison of what is known.

Choose one primary outcome per comparison:

| Decision | Outcome to examine |
| --- | --- |
| Concept or value proposition | Understanding the promised result and interest in pursuing it |
| Feature priority | Preference under a stated tradeoff or resource constraint |
| Free offer | Willingness to begin a specific useful task |
| Paid offer | Willingness to pay the stated price under the stated terms |
| Switching | Willingness to replace the current alternative, including switching effort |
| Continued use | Stated intention to repeat a particular action in a defined situation |

Define the action, conditions, and time horizon. Starting a trial, paying, switching, and returning are different outcomes. Do not combine their ratings or interpret one as evidence for another. Simulated return intent is not measured retention.

Record a study contract: run ID/date, decision, outcome, product/version, variant IDs, scenario IDs, evidence sources, comparison design, budget, model/settings when available, and assumptions. State what would favor an option and what would make the comparison inconclusive.

Default to two to four variants and three to five meaningfully different scenarios, with one initial reaction per scenario/variant cell. These are coverage choices, not a representative sample. Add matched repeats only to resolve a concrete stability question.

## 2. Prepare comparable offers

Build a factual stimulus card for each variant: intended user, problem, promised outcome, capabilities, requirements, limits, price, commitment, and next action. Mark material statements as supplied, verified, proposed, or unknown. Treat marketing claims as claims until verified.

Match presentation length, detail, visual polish, and available information unless presentation is the variable being tested. Use neutral variant labels and keep the founder's preferred option out of respondent instructions. Preserve brand information when it belongs to the intended decision context; record whether the comparison is branded or blinded.

Include a realistic current alternative: an existing product, manual process, doing nothing, or postponing. Preserve its actual costs and effort. For feature studies, include the current product without the addition. Do not engineer the comparison so that adoption is the only acceptable answer.

Normalize pricing before elicitation:

- Currency, region, billing period, upfront charge, renewal, taxes when known, and discounts.
- Per-user, team, unit, or usage basis; included allowances and likely overages.
- Common usage scenario and time horizon, with arithmetic shown.
- Trial, refund, cancellation, migration, and other material terms.

Show the annual upfront charge as well as any monthly equivalent. Do not describe annual commitment as monthly billing. Unknown charges and eligibility remain unknown. Do not assume paid status for a currently free product; label a new monetization proposal hypothetical.

If features, price, and positioning change together, label this a whole-offer comparison. It can compare packages but cannot identify which difference caused a reaction. Use controlled contrasts for attribution. Invent no current prices, supported capabilities, or commercially feasible margins.

## 3. Construct grounded scenarios

Describe each scenario through its job, current alternative, experience, urgency, usage frequency, budget constraints, decision authority, and switching effort. Include only attributes relevant to the decision.

Use supplied customer evidence where available. Otherwise label the scenario assumed and explain its role in coverage. Distinguish evidence about a segment from assumptions about its size or behavior. Avoid elaborate biographies and demographic stereotypes.

Include a low-fit or satisfied-current-user scenario when relevant. If the target audience is uncertain, compare audience hypotheses and preserve that uncertainty. Do not assume every scenario wants the product.

Specify any scenario weights before elicitation. Without credible prevalence information, default to scenario-level results. An equal-weight summary represents the chosen scenarios, not the market. Keep actual customer quotations linked to their source; generated reactions are never customer testimony.

## 4. Elicit independent, neutral reactions

Prefer a monadic design: each fresh respondent context sees one scenario, one offer, and its current alternative. Use the same scenario definitions across variants while keeping the responses isolated.

For a direct choice study, show the alternatives and status quo in a separate fresh context. Counterbalance or randomize order where supported and record actual order. Sequential price changes shown to one respondent are not independent price tests.

Provide only information available in the intended choice situation. Keep analyst findings, other responses, proposed fixes, desired answers, and scoring anchors out of respondent context.

Use a neutral request such as:

> You are a simulated respondent in the supplied scenario. Consider this offer under its stated conditions and your current alternative. How likely would you be to [specific action] within [time horizon]? Respond briefly in your own words without a numerical rating. Say when information is insufficient. Do not invent product facts or personal experiences.

Save the initial response before follow-ups. Then ask what informed it, what remains uncertain, which tradeoff matters, and what the respondent would do instead. Do not demand praise, objections, or a purchase. Permit choosing the current alternative, postponing, or withholding a judgment.

Use fresh agent contexts with task-local inputs when available. With one shared context, label the result an analyst scenario exercise; sequential role-play is not independent participation. Even separate model calls do not become independent human customers.

Preserve raw responses, prompt versions, scenario/variant IDs, order, available model settings, failures, and exclusions. Distinguish new elicited responses from analyst interpretations of supplied material. Never fabricate interviews, identities, quotes, timestamps, or tool outputs.

## 5. Optionally compute semantic similarity ratings

Use SSR when an ordinal intention summary helps and an authorized embedding tool or API is available. Otherwise proceed qualitatively and mark SSR not computed. Missing numeric scores must not prevent a useful provisional recommendation. Do not substitute guessed vectors, word matching, or an LLM-assigned score while calling it SSR.

The following adapts free-text elicitation and cosine mapping from [Maier et al. (2025), Appendix A.4.3, equations 7–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.08338). Their study evaluated personal-care concepts. Transfer to these products and outcomes requires validation; do not transfer the paper's headline accuracy. The [authors' implementation](https://github.com/pymc-labs/semantic-similarity-rating) is an optional reference, not a dependency of this file.

### Fixed mapping: Customer Lab SSR v1

Before seeing responses, freeze an action phrase that fits after "would" and describes the decision and horizon. For example: "buy this offer on its stated terms within the next 30 days". Keep detailed offer conditions in the stimulus so the same anchors can be used for all comparable variants.

Use these five anchors in order:

1. "I definitely would not [ACTION]."
2. "I probably would not [ACTION]."
3. "I am undecided about whether I would [ACTION]."
4. "I probably would [ACTION]."
5. "I definitely would [ACTION]."

Resolve placeholders once, save the exact strings, and use identical anchors for comparable cells. They must measure the declared action, not general sentiment. Changing the action creates a different instrument; do not combine scores for buying, trying, switching, or returning.

This version uses one anchor set, zero offset, and mapping temperature one. It is a declared adaptation, not a reproduction of the paper's six-set implementation.

Embed each saved initial intention response and the five anchors using the same actual embedding model, version, dimensions, and preprocessing. Record those settings. Score the initial intention statement, excluding follow-up commentary. If no interpretable intention was elicited, record insufficient information rather than coercing a rating.

For response vector `x` and anchor vectors `a[r]`, calculate with a computation tool:

```text
s[r] = dot(x, a[r]) / (norm(x) * norm(a[r]))
q[r] = s[r] - min(s)
p[r] = q[r] / sum(q)
```

Require five matching-dimension anchors and valid vectors. Reject missing, nonfinite, or zero-norm vectors. If `sum(q) <= 1e-12`, classify the response unmappable and report the exclusion. This threshold is an engineering convention for this version. Do not invent a uniform distribution or silently drop an excluded cell.

Retain response IDs, exact scored text, exact anchors, cosine similarities, mapped distributions, and exclusions. Verify probabilities are finite, nonnegative, and sum to one within numerical tolerance. An optional descriptive index is `sum(r * p[r])`, using `r = 1..5`. The mapped mass describes semantic placement on an ordinal scale; it is not a calibrated probability of purchase or other behavior.

Do not tune prompts, anchors, or parameters to favor a candidate. A change creates a new method version and requires recomputing all compared cells. Label alternate-anchor analyses as sensitivity checks and preserve original results. Validate any calibration on held-out human responses rather than reporting fit to calibration data as predictive accuracy.

## 6. Analyze differences and uncertainty

Use three evidence labels:

- **Observed:** A particular supplied or inspected statement, artifact, or actual interaction.
- **Simulated:** A generated interpretation, concern, intention, or choice.
- **Human-confirmed:** Identified actual customer research or behavior, with its source and scope.

Connect findings to the exact offer detail and response supporting them. Distinguish misunderstanding, insufficient information, low relevance, affordability, low credibility, switching effort, and preference for the current alternative. Do not force categories unsupported by the text.

Report scenario differences before any aggregate. Preserve dissent and neutrality. Counts require explicit denominators and wording such as "three of five simulated scenarios"; they are not customer percentages. A simple response count describes generated responses, not independent buyers.

When a decision depends on a small difference, repeat matched cells or vary presentation order while holding other inputs fixed. This tests model stability, not human sampling uncertainty. Do not manufacture confidence intervals or statistical significance from model repetition. A second model can expose model dependence; agreement is not independent human validation.

Treat close, inconsistent, confounded, or assumption-sensitive comparisons as inconclusive. Synthetic pricing reactions cannot establish an optimal price, market willingness to pay, revenue forecast, conversion lift, or retention. Give a provisional scenario-specific recommendation when the evidence supports one, even when the market-level decision remains unresolved.

## 7. Deliver an actionable report

Lead with a decision: advance an option to real-buyer validation, revise it, hold it, or resolve missing evidence. State the audience, conditions, and uncertainty behind the recommendation.

1. **Decision and scope:** Outcome, variants, scenarios, evidence mode, assumptions, exclusions.
2. **Comparison:** Normalized offers, status quo, controlled differences, remaining confounds.
3. **Scenario results:** Brief simulated reactions, perceived value, objections, alternative choice, response IDs.
4. **Changes:** Specific positioning, feature, package, or pricing hypotheses, with proposed wording where useful.
5. **Optional SSR:** Whether computed; method/version, embedding settings, exact anchors, results, exclusions, sensitivity.
6. **Next validation:** Smallest real-buyer study or observed-behavior check that resolves the main uncertainty.

Provide useful edits and preserve verified strengths. Label proposed claims and prices. Introduce no unsupported capabilities, testimonials, customer counts, or promises.

For concept and comprehension questions, propose real respondent checks. For purchase, activation, or retention, use the corresponding observed action as the eventual validation target. Keep a pilot's diagnostic value separate from a statistically powered commercial experiment. State what would change the recommendation.

Save requested reports and permitted supporting material under host rules. Do not contact customers, publish results, spend advertising budget, or execute transactions unless requested. No companion skill is required.

## Example requests

- "Compare these GamesLike value propositions against how people currently find games."
- "Assess these free Omnyo propositions for developers deciding whether to begin a first useful task."
- "Compare these Glassy UI template packages and Paraspeech offers using their supplied terms."
- "Evaluate these proposed Sledge features against the verified current experience."

Product names are examples, not a stored feature inventory.

## Completion check

Confirm the outcome is precise, offers are comparable, status quo is represented, scenario assumptions are visible, reactions remain identifiable as simulated, numbers were actually computed, and the recommendation identifies a concrete validation step with real buyers.

prompts.title: Check onboarding
prompts.body: Check onboarding on this build. Start as a new user and find your way to a useful first result. Show the biggest points of friction with evidence and steps to reproduce them. Leave the product unchanged.

prompts.title: Compare two offers
prompts.body: Compare these two offers for [audience]. Use the same buying situation for both, capture reactions in the buyers’ own words, and identify the objections worth testing with real customers.

layout.title: Customer Lab
layout.description: Find where people get stuck before you ship. Test a landing page, follow onboarding to the first useful result, try a product workflow or developer quickstart, and compare offers with simulated buyers.
